fixes.explanation: That would pull in a lot more men, and I get the thinking. But the LORD tells Moses and Aaron thirty to fifty for this work (Numbers 4:3). Fifty is the other end of the range, so there's a stopping point too. Think of a shift with a clock-in and a clock-out: thirty is clock-in, fifty is clock-out.

Counting is the census job, and in this passage the LORD hands that to Moses and Aaron (Numbers 4:2). The Kohathites are the ones being counted. Once the holy objects are covered and the camp is ready to move, the Kohathites come and do the carrying (Numbers 4:15). Counting gets them on the list, and carrying is the work.

False, and the text is plain about it. “But they must not touch the holy objects, or they will die.” (Numbers 4:15). Being careful isn't part of the verse at all. Aaron and his sons cover the holy objects first, and only then do the Kohathites come to carry (Numbers 4:15).

That's the one. Eleazar, Aaron's son, who served as a priest (Numbers 3:4), has oversight of the entire tabernacle and everything in it, including the holy objects and their utensils (Numbers 4:16). The oil, the incense and the grain offering are only part of his job. That's a lot to keep track of. I can barely keep track of one apron.

Battle? Not in this job description, friend. Eleazar served as a priest under his father Aaron (Numbers 3:4), and his list is the oil for the light, the fragrant incense, the daily grain offering and the anointing oil. Then comes the big one: oversight of the entire tabernacle and everything in it (Numbers 4:16). That's a workload for a man with a ring of keys, not a drill sergeant.

Food and water for the whole camp? I only run one oven and I'm already sweating. That job isn't handed to Eleazar here. He's Aaron's son, and he served as a priest (Numbers 3:4). His oversight is the oil, the incense, the daily grain offering and the anointing oil, and then the entire tabernacle and everything in it (Numbers 4:16).

Shields and spears aren't on the Gershonites' list. What they carry is the curtains of the tabernacle, the Tent of Meeting with its covering of fine leather, and the curtains of the courtyard, along with their ropes and equipment (Numbers 4:25-26). This is carrying work for the Tent of Meeting, not fighting work.

Baskets and sacks aren't on the Merarites' list. What is on it? The frames of the tabernacle with its crossbars, posts and bases (Numbers 4:31). Then the posts of the surrounding courtyard with their bases, tent pegs and ropes (Numbers 4:32). That's frames, posts, pegs and ropes.

Yes. The LORD says, “You shall assign by name the items that they are responsible to carry.” (Numbers 4:32). With that many pieces, I think assigning by name keeps everybody clear on what's theirs. I wish my kitchen drawers ran like that.

True. Ithamar, Aaron's son, who served as a priest (Numbers 3:4), directs both clans. The Gershonites' duties are under his direction (Numbers 4:28), and so is the work of the Merarites (Numbers 4:33). One director, two clans. That's a big stack of tent gear for one man to keep track of.

It's actually the same man for both. Ithamar, Aaron's son, who served as a priest (Numbers 3:4), directs the Gershonites (Numbers 4:28). The Merarites' work is also under the direction of Ithamar (Numbers 4:33). So he has a lot on his plate, and I bet he stayed busy.

That's not what the text says. It counts the Kohathites, the Gershonites and the Merarites, the men from thirty to fifty who came to serve, and the number was 8,580 (Numbers 4:46-48). Then it says, “At the LORD’s command through Moses they were numbered, and each one was assigned his work and burden, as the LORD had commanded Moses.” (Numbers 4:49). So the work goes to every counted man, and it doesn't stop at one clan.

False. All three clans are counted, and the men from thirty to fifty who came to serve number 8,580 (Numbers 4:46-48). Then the text says, “…each one was assigned his work and burden, as the LORD had commanded Moses.” (Numbers 4:49). Each one means each one. Every counted man gets a job, and that's about the best news a man can hear.
